procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the 2nd Munsif at Arrah
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 4th day of May 1949 of the High Court of Judicature at Patna in Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 1918 of 1947
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The case originated in the Court of the 2nd Munsif at Arrah in Suit No. T.S. 120 of 1943, which issued a Decree dated the 29th March 1946. This decree was appealed to the Subordinate Judge at Arrah in Appeal No. 137 of 1946, which issued a Decree dated the 23rd day of July 1947. This decree was further appealed to the High Court of Judicature at Patna in Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 1918 of 1947, which issued the Judgment and Order dated the 4th day of May 1949.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The case reached the Supreme Court by Special Leave Appeal. The Supreme Court reversed the Judgment of the High Court of Patna.

issue.issue_text: Whether a female heir has a right to succeed to an office by getting the duties of the office performed by the next male in succession.

facts: A female plaintiff claimed the right to inherit a share in a hereditary priestly office (Pujari and Panda).

The defendant objected, arguing that a female is barred by religion, custom, and usage from inheriting such an office and cannot perform the duties either personally or through a representative ('karinda').
law: The Court referenced the principle that there is no general prohibition in Hindu law or established custom that disqualifies a female from succeeding to a hereditary religious office.
It cited a Privy Council decision which held that a woman can hold a religious office so long as the duties, if she cannot perform them herself, can be discharged by a deputy.

The Court noted that precedents from various High Courts (Madras, Calcutta) and the prevalence of the practice in states like Bengal and Bihar supported the usage of female succession to priestly offices with the duties being performed by a proxy.
application: The Court found that the defendant had failed to provide any authority or prove any custom to show that a female cannot inherit an office of this nature.
It observed that the practice of females succeeding to such offices and appointing a substitute was so common and well-recognized that it was often not contested in court.

Applying the Privy Council's test, the Court determined that the crucial question was not whether the female could perform the duties personally, but whether the duties could be performed by a deputy. Since they could, her sex was not a bar to inheritance.
The Court affirmed the lower appellate court's view that a female is not disqualified and can get the duties performed by a proxy, who would typically be the next male in the line of succession.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a female heir has a right to succeed to a hereditary priestly office. It held that she is not disqualified by Hindu law or custom and is entitled to get the duties, which she may be barred from performing personally due to her sex, carried out by a suitable male proxy.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a female heir has a right to succeed to an office by getting the duties of the office performed by the next male in succession.
appellant_arguments: The plaintiff-appellant is entitled to succeed to the office.
It is a matter of general knowledge and experience that service in temples is performed by proxies, which would allow a female heir to hold the office while a male performs the duties.
Numerous High Courts have previously acted on the assumption that female heirs, such as a widow or daughter, can succeed to such offices.
The respondent's own plea regarding a partition of offices for another temple implies a recognition of the plaintiff's right to succeed, which contradicts their current argument.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not explicitly detailed but can be inferred from the context that they opposed the appellant's claim, likely arguing that a female heir was not entitled to succeed to the office.
The respondent made a plea in the written statement, but no evidence was provided to support it.

cases.principle: Cited for the statement that High Courts have, in numerous cases, acted on the assumption of the peculiar nature of certain offices which combine both the element of property and the element of duty.
Cited for a passage from a trial court judgment that was quoted with apparent approval by the Judicial Committee.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A usage, even if it is sanctioned, ought not to be recognised by courts.
obiter: The peculiar nature of such offices combines in them both the element of property and the element of duty.
A right to succeed by getting the duties of the office performed by the next male in succession.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A female heir has a right to succeed to a hereditary priestly office and get the duties performed by a competent deputy. This right is based on a well-recognized usage that is not contradicted by textual Hindu law. The right to the office is an element of property, and while it is combined with an element of duty, public policy concerns are met by ensuring the proper and efficient discharge of those duties through oversight, rather than by negating the hereditary right itself. This right can only be defeated in cases where a specific usage to the contrary is both pleaded and established with evidence.
legal_tests_applied: A female heir is entitled to succeed to a hereditary office and appoint a substitute unless the opposing party pleads and proves a specific usage to the contrary.
why_respondent_won: The usage of a female succeeding to a priestly office and having the duties performed by a competent deputy is well-recognized in case law.
There is nothing in textual Hindu law that prohibits a female from succeeding to such an office.
Numerous High Courts have previously acted on the assumption that female heirs, such as a widow or daughter, can succeed to such offices.
The respondent pleaded a contrary usage but failed to provide any evidence to establish it, thus failing to meet their burden of proof.
policy_considerations: In offices that combine both an element of property and an element of duty, the consideration of public policy cannot be insisted on to the extent of negating the property right itself, especially where there is no express prohibition.

Public policy is sufficiently served by emphasizing the duty-aspect of the office and allowing temple authorities or other interested parties to enforce the proper and efficient performance of services, rather than by denying the right of succession to a female heir.
